content.text: Electric motors power countless devices in our daily lives—from the fan in your computer to the starter motor in a car. DC (direct current) motors convert electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy using the motor effect. Understanding how they work reveals the elegant application of electromagnetic principles.

A DC motor converts electrical energy into rotational kinetic energy using the motor effect. The commutator (split ring) reverses the current every half turn to keep the coil spinning continuously in the same direction.
A DC motor converts electrical energy to kinetic energy (rotation) using the motor effect:
Current flows through a coil in a magnetic field
Motor effect creates forces on the coil sides
Forces act in opposite directions, creating rotation
Commutator reverses current to maintain rotation
Wound on an iron core for stronger field
Reverses current direction every half turn

When explaining how a DC motor works, always mention five key components: magnets, coil, commutator, brushes, and axle. Explain what each does, especially the commutator -- it is the most commonly tested component.
A DC motor coil has current flowing as shown. The magnetic field points from left to right. Describe the forces on the coil and the resulting motion.
Top of coil: current out of page, field right → force upward
Bottom of coil: current into page, field right → force downward
The forces create a clockwise rotation (viewed from the front).
Explain why a DC motor without a commutator would not spin continuously.
Coil rotates due to initial forces
After half rotation, the coil sides have swapped positions
Without current reversal, forces are now opposite
The commutator reverses the current each half turn, ensuring forces always create rotation in the same direction.
Suggest two ways to make a DC motor spin faster.
(Also acceptable: reduce mechanical load, reduce coil resistance)
Motors are not 100% efficient. Energy losses include:
— Motors convert electrical energy TO kinetic energy. Generators do the opposite.
— Too much voltage causes overheating and damage.
— In most DC motors, the magnet is fixed. The coil (armature) rotates.
— They use the same magnetic principles, but electronic circuits replace mechanical commutators.
— They easily reverse by changing current or field direction.

A motor and a generator are essentially the same device working in reverse. A motor uses electricity to produce motion; a generator uses motion to produce electricity. Both rely on the interaction between a magnetic field and a current-carrying conductor.

DC motor converts electrical energy to kinetic energy
Components: magnets, coil/armature, commutator, brushes, axle
Motor effect creates forces on current-carrying coil
Commutator reverses current every half turn for continuous rotation
Speed increases with: higher voltage, stronger magnets, less load
Torque increases with: more current, stronger field, more turns
Direction reversed by: reversing current OR reversing field
Energy losses: heating, friction, sound, eddy currents
Permanent magnets, coil (armature), commutator (split ring), brushes.
— The axle is also acceptable as a fifth component. (recall)
The commutator reverses the direction of current through the coil every half turn, ensuring the forces always produce rotation in the same direction.
The brushes are stationary carbon contacts that maintain electrical connection between the rotating commutator and the external power supply.
Use Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger points left (field), second finger from X to Y (current). The thumb gives the direction of the force — upward.
Increase the current (e.g. higher voltage) and use stronger magnets. Also valid: increase the number of turns or add an iron core.

Electrical energy is transferred to kinetic energy but also to thermal energy due to: resistance heating in the coil wires (I²R losses), friction at the brushes and bearings, and eddy currents in metal parts.

The commutator is likely missing, broken, or not making proper contact. Without the commutator reversing the current every half turn, forces reverse after 180° and the coil oscillates. Fix by adding or repairing the split-ring commutator.
Brushed: simpler and cheaper, but brushes wear out and can spark. Brushless: more efficient, longer lasting, and quieter, but more expensive and require electronic control circuitry.
